newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND-Global stocks face tough 97, eyes on Europe.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Global stocks face tough 97, eyes on Europe.

text.p: Wall Street stole the show in the 1996 global stock markets arena but continental Europe and wildcard Japan may grab the spotlight if their economies rebound further in what is expected to be a tough 1997.

Analysts said savvy investors will turn to early business cycle stocks amid signs of economic recovery in individual countries as sector selection becomes more key than which nation or area to invest in.
"1997 will be a very tough year," said Daniel Duane, head of global mutual fund products at Prudential Mutual Funds.

Leila Heckman, a managing director at Smith Barney, recommends an "overweighting in emerging markets relative to capitalization -- emerging Europe as well as, more modestly, Asia ex-Japan. In developed countries we would more overweight Europe than Japan."
"We like Latin America for the cheap valuations but they're not as cheap as this time last year," she added.

When asked about Peru's ongoing hostage crisis, analysts shrugged it off as a function of investing in an emerging market and stressed diversification. The Lima stock exchange re-opened Thursday after trade was suspended Wednesday on a sharp drop.

As for the United States, where the Dow industrials rose 34 percent in 1995 and is up 23 percent so far this year, analysts pointed to high but not outrageous valuations and several suggested to be ready to buy on large dips.
But Morgan Stanley's global strategist Barton Biggs warned that 1997 will be the toughest year that equities have faced since 1990 and may represent the early stage of a bear market.

In a report, Biggs said he was "selling stocks around the world," principally in the U.S. He cut his exposure in Europe and Hong Kong on the belief that if the U.S. market tails off, "it will bring down some of the other high-fliers around the world with it."

Merrill Lynch was also wary. In a recent report, it said, "We would be alert to the idea that an upcoming peak in the post-July global equity rally could also mark the completion of the post-1994 bull market. As a result, the potential for a difficult 1997 is expected to be global in nature."
Japan's prospects were a subject of great debate.

"One country that screams out as unbelievably cheap is Japan. There is such a pervasive bear market mentality in Japan. It probably is not going to go down a lot but at some point in will turn and when it does -- it'll be explosive," Prudential's Duane said.
Japan's Nikkei 225 has risen three percent so far in 1996 and a Reuters poll showed analysts expect the index to rise by a mean of 14 percent in 1997.
Still, as Duane said, other analysts who were burned by fallen hopes for a stronger 1996 rebound in Japanese equities remain cautious about Tokyo's market.

"We're not bullish on Japan and would recommend an underweighting. I do think the economy will decelerate. Small caps and the financial sector and mid-tiers have not performed as well," said Joseph Quinlan, a senior international economist at Dean Witter.

"We were more positive on Japan last year. But it seems to be stuck in a quagmire. An easier credit policy is not the answer. It's not moving aggressively to open markets and unemployment is near a record high. Consumer spending is contracting again," Quinlan said.

As for other stock markets, much of the number crunching and forecasts also rely on analysts' views for the dollar, which has been steadily appreciating. For 1997, analysts generally see the dollar posting more gains against the mark and yen and then drifting below current levels by year-end.

Ron Chapman, head of international equities at Dreyfus Corp, noted that over the past dozen years, periods when U.S. stocks have underperformed other world markets have coincided with a declining dollar. At the same time, outperformance by foreign stocks corresponds with good performance by the Japanese market, he said.

Weighing heavily in Chapman's 1997 forecast is a renewed slide in the dollar. He said despite the strength in the dollar over the last 18 to 24 months, factors that have caused the dollar to be chronically weak over a 25-year period have not changed. Reasons to anticipate a lower dollar, he said, include a continuation of high U.S. trade deficits and the flow of dollars for real investment moving from the U.S. to overseas locations.
Because a dollar decline adds to return for international investors, Chapman argued this is another reason for overseas markets to look relatively more attractive.
Looking ahead to 1997, Chapman expects foreign stocks to at least keep up with U.S. stocks. "In light of the last two years (for U.S. stocks) that's saying something," he said.

Meanwhile, Europe faces a crucial time as it moves toward a single currency. "In 1997, it's crunch time for Europe," Dean Witter's Quinlan said. He sees a "restructuring play in Europe that's just start of the ballgame," favoring Germany.

As for sectors, Prudential's Duane said, "The key is not so much a country thing but you have to watch and monitor sector rotation. In continental Europe, secular growth stocks in the context of a market that's pretty inexpensive -- medium-sized techs have really stretched valuations. At the first sign of economic recovery, there will be a very strong rotation to early business cycle companies."
"It will be very important to own beneficiaries of consumer companies in continental Europe," he said.
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
